the-future-of-real-estate.synopsis: In this video podcast episode, Sean Stewart of Stewart & Co. Real Estate sits down with interior designer and developer Alex Sandeman at Sandy Cove on Barbados’ Platinum Coast. Alex discusses modern Caribbean design, construction challenges, sustainability, and what overseas buyers should know before renovating or building property in Barbados. Drawing on decades of experience in both development and professional golf, Alex offers practical advice on creating durable, lifestyle-focused homes in a tropical climate.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: Before we dive into design and development, tell us a bit about yourself. What drives you professionally?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Over the last 30 years, different things have motivated me. I grew up in England and have lived in Barbados for 25 years. I had a career in golf, but I’ve always loved building and interior design. I’m driven by the desire to improve everything I do.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: You’re also known for holding a Guinness World Record for making 93 birdies in 12 hours. How did that come about?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Only one record, but I’ve held it twice. As my golf career was winding down and I was getting more involved in development, I attempted the birdie record at Sandy Lane in 2010. Someone broke it in 2013, so I went back and reclaimed it. It kept me motivated, and I enjoyed the physical challenge.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: Is there anything you’ve taken from golf and applied to development and interior design?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: My downfall in golf was being a perfectionist, which isn’t great for performance. But in design and development, that same pursuit of perfection works in my favour. It helps me maintain the standard I want to achieve.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: We’re sitting in one of your projects, a 3,000 sq. ft. apartment at Sandy Cove. What was involved in renovating this space?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: We finished this about a year ago. It hadn’t been renovated since it was built 15 or 16 years ago. We had only two months because of restrictions on noisy work, so preparation was everything. We redid the floors, bathrooms, and pretty much everything. It was a big job, but it turned out great.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: What other projects are you currently working on?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: We’re about to start a major renovation on an 8,500 sq. ft. villa at Sandy Lane. We’re also building four new five-bedroom villas at Porters Place Residences, Phase Two, and we have several other projects in the pipeline.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: How would you describe the design aesthetic in Barbados today?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: There’s a strong move towards sleek, modern design, although I personally love both modern and classic styles. Maintenance plays a huge role here. Modern materials like aluminium windows and doors tend to perform better in this climate.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: Do modern construction methods help with hurricane resistance?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Definitely. Flat concrete roofs are now very common. They’re stronger, allow space for services and PV panels, and require less maintenance than traditional pitched roofs.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: What design mistakes do you see most often?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Maintenance is the big one. Homeowners want lower running costs and manageable communal fees. Designing for durability is essential in the Caribbean.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: What are overseas buyers generally looking for?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: It varies. Some want large family villas, others want compact apartments. Retirees, families, and investors all have different needs, but the general direction we’re heading seems to suit most buyers.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: How important is sustainability in Barbados?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Very important. We’re using more photovoltaic systems and trying to make better use of our climate. It’s a learning process, and progress is slower than we’d like, but it’s improving.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: What advice would you give someone planning a renovation or build in Barbados?

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: What do people most underestimate?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: How challenging it is. Even with experience, we’re still learning. But if you get it right, Barbados is an incredible place to live.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: How do you see sport, especially golf, impacting tourism in Barbados?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Barbados has become a serious golf destination. We now have several world-class courses. Places like Apes Hill offer a full lifestyle experience that appeals to families and long-term visitors, not just golfers.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: Are you seeing more demand for wellness-focused developments?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Yes. We have a project in development that includes a wellness centre with a gym, spa, cold plunge, and paddle courts. Demand for wellness facilities is growing across the island.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: Where can people find out more about your work?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Through Alex Sandeman Design. We handle design and project management for our own developments and for private clients. We’re on Instagram, and our website is alexsandeman.com.

transcript.speaker: Sean
transcript.text: Final advice for anyone buying or building in Barbados?

transcript.speaker: Alex
transcript.text: Build a strong team. Architect, engineer, contractor, interior designer, and landscape architect. Some people try to do it alone, but it’s more complex than it looks. Having the right team makes all the difference.

buying-property-in-barbados-legal-insigh.synopsis: In this interview, Sean Stewart of Stewart & Co Real Estate speaks with three members of the Barbados law firm Harridyal Sodha Associates. The conversation explores the legal realities behind property transactions on the island, from title searches and due diligence to financing, estate planning, and ownership structures.

transcript.speaker: Sean Stewart
transcript.text: Hi everyone, Sean here at Stewart & Co Real Estate. Today I'm joined by not one, not two, but three members of the law firm Harridyal Sodha Associates. Liza Harridyal, Keisha Hyde-Porchetta, and Ayo Barnard-Rollins are going to tell me all about various aspects of law relating to property transactions in Barbados.

transcript.speaker: Sean Stewart
transcript.text: For someone buying or investing in Barbados for the first time, what’s the biggest thing they should understand about how the legal process works here?

transcript.speaker: Liza Harridyal
transcript.text: I’ll start by explaining our roles in the firm. I’m the principal of the firm. Ayo is the vice-principal and also the head of our real estate department, and Keisha is the head of our corporate department.

transcript.speaker: Liza Harridyal
transcript.text: The delays are not usually because professionals are slow. Much of the process depends on manual systems and government departments, which means attorneys often have to wait for documentation or searches to be completed.

transcript.speaker: Sean Stewart
transcript.text: That’s important to understand, especially if a buyer is coordinating a purchase here with another transaction overseas.

transcript.speaker: Liza Harridyal
transcript.text: Barbados operates largely under an unregistered land system. That means attorneys must investigate the chain of title by reviewing historical deeds.

transcript.speaker: Sean Stewart
transcript.text: What are the most common misconceptions foreign buyers have?

transcript.speaker: Sean Stewart
transcript.text: We’re seeing more buyers use companies or trusts to hold property. When does that make sense?

transcript.speaker: Sean Stewart
transcript.text: When it comes to development projects, what challenges do developers underestimate?

transcript.speaker: Liza Harridyal
transcript.text: Budget and timing. Those are always the two biggest issues.

transcript.speaker: Liza Harridyal
transcript.text: Foreign buyers can obtain mortgages in Barbados, although typically banks may lend around fifty percent of the property value depending on the circumstances.

transcript.speaker: Sean Stewart
transcript.text: Thank you all for sharing your insights. This has been extremely helpful for anyone interested in buying property in Barbados.
